title: LTS branch cut planning notes (runtime-1.20-lts) — open questions, timeline, customer language
content:
Doc intent
- Working notes for the first Runtime LTS cut (target: runtime-1.20-lts). This is not the final ADR/policy.
- Primary outputs from this doc:
  1) crisp branch cut plan (when/what/owners)
  2) list of open decisions to close in the ADR + backport policy
  3) draft customer-facing language for “slower change” promise

Last updated summary (2025-12-10)
- Proposed cut: runtime-1.20-lts.0, with a 1-week stabilization window before declaring GA for pilot accounts.
- Release Eng is aligned on tooling direction (labels + backport automation + signing). SRE wants perf gates to be “hard” for LTS RCs.
- Open: exact support window length (12 vs 18 months), and how we communicate compatibility guarantees without over-promising.

Why we’re doing this (context)
- Enterprise Dedicated/Private customers are asking for a stable runtime line with predictable change rate.
- Support tickets show churn due to minor upgrades and noisy release notes:
  - SUP-3921: customer asks for LTS track for Private
  - SUP-3950: regression after minor upgrade; prefers backport instead of another upgrade
  - SUP-3988: wants clearer notes + risk tagging

Definition of “first LTS cut”
- A new branch off runtime release line at runtime 1.20 (exact tag TBD).
- LTS gets:
  - slower patch cadence (predictable)
  - clearly defined backport policy (what qualifies + how it’s tested)
  - enterprise-style release notes focused on operational impact
  - stronger release evidence (artifact signing + traceability)
- LTS does NOT get:
  - features-by-request
  - broad refactors / internal cleanup
  - experimental kernels / scheduler changes without clear correctness/perf justification

Proposed branch naming + versioning
- Git branch name: runtime-1.20-lts
- Patch tag examples:
  - runtime-1.20-lts.0 (initial cut)
  - runtime-1.20-lts.1 (first patch)
  - runtime-1.20-lts.2 …
- NOTE: Align with Private installer semantics (Vivek) and artifact naming in registries (Sahana + Connor).

Candidate cut criteria (draft)
- Cut from a runtime 1.20.x tag that meets:
  - CI: green on standard runtime release CI
  - determinism checks: passing (if we’re enforcing for LTS artifacts)
  - perf-canary baseline: within thresholds on agreed benchmark set
  - no open Sev0/Sev1 issues in runtime related to kernel/scheduling correctness
- If we can’t meet all criteria by target date, we either:
  - delay cut by up to 1 week, OR
  - cut but declare “pilot only” until gates are met (strong preference: don’t cut until gates are met)

Support window (open decision)
- Options being discussed:
  1) 12 months from branch cut date, with 3 additional months for security-only
  2) 18 months from branch cut date, with final quarter security-only
- Considerations:
  - Product wants commitments to be simple and competitive (Lauren / Vivek input)
  - Runtime wants to avoid supporting too many lines simultaneously
  - Compliance wants a clear policy on security patches and evidence collection (Naomi)
- Action: Noah to propose recommendation in ADR language with rationale + resourcing implications.

Patch cadence (draft)
- Regular cadence: every 2 weeks for patch release if there are eligible changes; otherwise “no-op” note or skip.
- Out-of-band: emergency patches for Sev0/critical security (within 24–72 hours depending on repro + gate completion).
- Open: do we commit to a minimum cadence (e.g., monthly) even if no changes? My take: publish “no changes” note monthly, but don’t force patch tags.

Backport intake + queue (draft workflow)
- Entry points:
  - Runtime PRs that are labeled needs-backport
  - Support escalations mapped to Jira tickets (SUP-*) + Linear task created for traceability
  - Security embargo items (restricted path)
- Triage meeting proposal (30 min, weekly):
  - Owner: Omar (runtime backport owner)
  - Required attendees: release eng (Connor), runtime (Sofia or Hiro depending), SRE gate owner (Sean or delegate) when perf risk is involved
- Queue tracking:
  - Use the Drive tracker sheet (runtime-lts-backport-queue-tracker) until automation is fully in place.

Risk tiers (draft)
- Tier 0: Security-critical / exploited / critical CVSS — expedite, restricted comms, additional signing evidence.
- Tier 1: Correctness bug causing wrong outputs, crashes, deadlocks, data corruption.
- Tier 2: Perf regression vs baseline (p95/p99 or throughput) impacting SLOs.
- Tier 3: “nice to have” (minor perf improvements, minor stability improvements) — likely excluded for first 1–2 patches unless very low risk.
- Explicitly excluded for LTS:
  - refactors for readability
  - feature flags / new config surfaces without enterprise need
  - “perf improvements” that change scheduling behavior materially without robust canary evidence

SRE gates and canary plan (draft)
- Owners:
  - Gate definition: Sean
  - Canary execution template: Miles
- Gate summary (to be formalized in SRE doc):
  - Perf: thresholds for p95 AND p99 latency plus throughput regression limits vs LTS baseline.
  - Stability: error-rate and OOM rate thresholds.
  - Canary duration: minimum 6 hours, prefer 24 hours for non-emergency.
  - Rollback criteria: any Sev1 or repeated alert storms attributable to runtime change; perf regression beyond threshold; unexplained crash loop.
- Open: what is “enough canary” for emergency security patch? Proposal: 1–2 hours + targeted tests + follow-up extended canary.

CI / build / artifact provenance (draft)
- Owners: Sahana (CI), Connor (release), Marcus Lin (security review for signing), Olga Petrov (audit evidence expectations)
- Requirements we believe we need for LTS artifacts:
  - reproducible build or “deterministic enough” build + recorded build environment
  - signed artifacts (image + tarballs) and stored attestations
  - traceability: issue -> PR -> backport PR -> tag -> artifact digest
- Open:
  - Where do we store attestations long-term? (compliance retention)
  - Is cosign/SLSA level called out in customer language, or internal-only?

Private installer / Helm alignment
- Owners: Vivek (product), Kira Thompson (docs), release eng support from Connor
- Requirements for the cut:
  - Private installer can pin runtime-1.20-lts.* and validate artifact digests
  - Document supported upgrade paths:
    - runtime-1.20.x -> runtime-1.20-lts.0 (yes)
    - runtime-1.19.x -> runtime-1.20-lts.0 (maybe, but we should strongly recommend a staged upgrade)
  - Rollback guidance must be explicit (what state is safe, how to validate)
- Open: do we support direct jump from older minors into LTS? Product wants it, runtime worries about hidden incompatibilities. Likely: “best effort” with documented guardrails.

Timeline proposal (for first cut)
- Week 0 (now): finalize cut criteria + owners; start backport queue hygiene.
- Week 1:
  - land branch tooling + branch protections (PR #8421)
  - land backport labels/templates (PR #8429)
  - confirm benchmark set + baseline versioning (perf-canary PR #311, benchmark-lab PR #522)
- Week 2:
  - cut runtime-1.20-lts branch
  - produce runtime-1.20-lts.0 RC
  - run CI + perf gates + canary
- Week 3:
  - publish runtime-1.20-lts.0
  - pilot on 1–2 internal environments + select enterprise account(s)
  - collect feedback on release notes clarity (Elliot)

Owners / DRIs (draft)
- Overall release train + go/no-go: Connor O’Brien
- LTS architecture / branching decision text: Noah Patel
- Backport triage + conflict resolution: Omar El-Sayed
- Scheduling sign-off (risky scheduler changes): Sofia Ivanova
- Kernel sign-off (kernel/perf changes): Hiro Tanaka
- CI + build determinism + matrix: Sahana Iyer
- Perf regression gate thresholds: Sean Gallagher
- Canary/rollback runbook: Miles Thornton
- Private upgrade/rollback guidance: Kira Thompson
- Enterprise release notes template + polish: Elliot Price
- Compliance/audit evidence expectations: Olga Petrov (with Marcus Lin for signing/provenance)

Open questions (need answers before we tell customers anything)
1) Support window: 12 vs 18 months; do we add “security-only tail”?
2) Compatibility guarantees:
   - What exactly is guaranteed stable? (API surface? model configs? kernel behavior?)
   - Are there any known exceptions (e.g., emergency security patch that changes behavior)?
3) Backport rules for perf:
   - Do we allow perf improvements that are not strictly regressions? (probably “rarely”)
4) Branch cut source:
   - Do we cut from 1.20.0, 1.20.1, or a later stable tag?
5) Private deployment path:
   - What is the oldest supported “upgrade into LTS” version we can commit to?
6) Emergency patch process:
   - What gates are mandatory vs “best effort” under Sev0? Who signs off?
7) How do we label change risk in release notes consistently?

Draft customer-facing language (working copy; needs Product + Legal/Comms review)

Option A (short)
“Redwood Runtime LTS is a long-term supported runtime line designed for teams that prioritize operational stability. LTS releases follow a slower change cadence and focus on high-confidence fixes: security patches, correctness issues, and narrowly scoped stability/performance regressions. Each LTS patch includes enterprise-grade release notes that summarize what changed, why it matters, and upgrade risk.”

Option B (more explicit)
“Runtime LTS provides a stable runtime track with predictable patch releases. We keep change low by limiting LTS patches to:
- security fixes
- correctness fixes
- stability fixes
- targeted performance regressions (when measured against the LTS baseline)
We do not introduce new features or large refactors in LTS patches. Every patch is validated through an LTS-specific test and canary process and includes clear, operational release notes (impact, risk level, known issues, and mitigations).”

Option C (includes deployment modes)
“Runtime LTS is intended for Dedicated and Private deployments that need fewer upgrades and clearer operational visibility. LTS artifacts are published with predictable versioning and are supported by upgrade and rollback guidance for Private environments.”

Language we should avoid (risk of over-commitment)
- “No behavior changes” (we can’t guarantee this in all cases)
- “Zero downtime upgrades” (depends on customer topology)
- “All fixes will be backported” (we need eligibility + risk tier policy)
- “Same performance always” (we can say ‘no regressions beyond thresholds’)

Notes to self (Connor)
- Make sure the customer language aligns with what Support can actually defend during escalations.
- Need a crisp answer to: “If I’m on LTS, do I ever need to take a non-LTS upgrade?” (probably: only if out of support window or if fix is ineligible/risky).

Next steps
- Noah: propose support window recommendation + compatibility guarantees text (for ADR draft).
- Sahana/Connor: confirm LTS CI required checks list and what is blocking enforcement (determinism + signing).
- Sean/Miles: finalize perf thresholds and minimum canary duration for normal vs emergency patches.
- Vivek/Kira T.: lock Private upgrade/rollback guidance scope for pilot (what versions supported, what we document).
- Elliot: convert draft release notes template into “LTS notes” structure (what’s changed, why it matters, risk level, mitigations) and sanity check against SUP-3988 feedback.

Appendix: Meeting notes snippets (raw)
- 2025-12-02 (Runtime + Release Eng): We need a hard line against refactors. If a fix requires refactor, it’s probably not LTS-eligible unless it’s the only safe path.
- 2025-12-05 (SRE): Perf gates must include p99, not just p95, or we’ll ship tail latency regressions into the exact customers who care most.
- 2025-12-06 (Private Product): Customers want “pick one version and stop thinking about it.” We should promise predictability and clear comms, not indefinite support.
